new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in Temiar (and Semai) is fixed on the word-final syllable, which is always a full ('major', heavy CVC) syllable; pre-final 'minor' (vowelless/epenthetic) syllables never bear stress; the canonical word is a sesquisyllabic iamb with final prominence. Data explicitly taken from Benjamin (1976) 'An outline of Temiar grammar' and Diffloth (1976a,b) (fn. 2, p. 44).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; fn. 29 (p. 77) says stress 'usually falls only on the word-final position' and that no decisive data exist on whether a reduplicated heavy syllable (Type 5 suffixal reduplication) also carries stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Only the open question in fn. 29 about possible stress on both base and reduplicant in heavy-syllable reduplication ('no decisive data available').
new_statements.identity_note: Miyakoshi 2006 treats Temiar and Semai together as 'Aslian' and draws all Temiar data from Benjamin (1976) 'An outline of Temiar grammar'; no particular Temiar dialect is named.

sources.citation: Matisoff, James A. 2003. Aslian: Mon-Khmer of the Malay Peninsula. Mon-Khmer Studies 33: 1-58 (with embedded comments by G. Benjamin).
sources.quote: 'Sesquisyllabic forms consist of a "major" syllable with fully-stressed vowel, preceded by a "minor" syllable with predictable vocalism (e.g. Temiar ... )'; 'Truly disyllabic words have non-predictable vowels in their non-final syllables. In these cases, even if the non-final vowel is unstressed (e.g. "monitor lizard" Semai ..., Temiar kabug, Jah Hut kabok) ...'; 'Disyllabic compounds with unreduced though unstressed vowels also occur (e.g. Temiar diŋ-rab "shelter").' I.e. stress on the final (major) syllable, non-final syllables unstressed, Temiar cited explicitly.
